title: The Power Broker
blurb: Caro's 1,300-page life of Robert Moses is the definitive anatomy of power: how it is accumulated, exercised, and hidden in plain sight. Long, but never long enough.

title: I, Pencil
blurb: A pencil explains its own creation and dismantles the idea that anyone is in charge. The shortest, sharpest case for spontaneous order ever written.

title: 12 Angry Men
blurb: Twelve strangers, one sweltering room, and a single dissenter who refuses to let certainty win. Still the best film ever made about the discipline of doubt.

title: Aspiration and the Examined Life
blurb: Agnes Callard argues that the biggest decisions in life cannot be justified in advance — aspiration means becoming the person who can see the reasons only afterward. Bracing and oddly comforting.

title: Democracy in America
blurb: Sent to study American prisons, Tocqueville instead diagnosed a young democracy with uncanny precision. Nearly two centuries later, almost every page feels like this morning's news.

title: Politics and the English Language
blurb: Orwell shows how mushy language and mushy thinking prop each other up, then hands you the tools to resist both. The rare essay on style you can read for pleasure.

title: Spotlight
blurb: A newspaper procedural with the pulse of a thriller — and a quiet lesson that institutions change only when someone keeps asking uncomfortable questions.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
blurb: A career's worth of findings about judgment, bias, and self-deception in one humane, humbling book. You will catch yourself in the act by chapter three.

title: Michael Sandel on the Tyranny of Merit
blurb: What shouldn't money buy? Sandel and Roberts disagree productively about markets, merit, and manners in a conversation that models civil argument.

title: The Case for Reparations
blurb: History, housing policy, and one Chicago family's story braided into the most consequential essay of its decade. Read it for the argument — and stay for the craft.

title: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
blurb: Ford's elegy for the West asks what a civilization owes the legends it prints. "When the legend becomes fact, print the legend" — cinema's coldest sentence.

title: The Road to Serfdom
blurb: Written in the middle of a world war, Hayek's warning about planning, expertise, and liberty still infuriates and illuminates in equal measure.

title: The Fall of Rome
blurb: Two historians thrash out barbarians, taxes, and bronze coinage with infectious delight, and make the fifth century feel like breaking news.
